bearings.paper_claim: IM-CSN as edge activation: fixed seed set, each node may activate at most k of its out-edges (k in 5, 10, 20), reward is marginal IC spread. A trained Double DQN edge policy beats Random, Degree and FoF in 462, 464 and 462 of 480 configurations and PSNA in 456 of 480. Abstract says up to 15% higher spread; Sec 6.3 says improvements frequently exceed 15%, so the two statements differ.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3 problem formulation (fixed seed set S, out-degree budget k); Sec 5.1 MDP; Sec 6.2 Q1-Q2 and Fig 3; Sec 6.3 and Fig 6; Abstract
bearings.system_side: Docstring credits 'RELINK + MOPBD*' (cosponsor_route.py line 3). Champions are seeds and each recruiter whips at most K=5 colleagues (K env default 5, line 9). Greedy route for lambda in 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 on value-per-dollar (gain - lambda(1-p))/cost, then a Pareto front. Optional MC reach runs only when MCMODE=1 (off by default). K=5 and CEDGE=10000 are unestimated env defaults.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the framing transfers: edge actions under a per-node budget. The paper's numbers are for a trained DDQN policy on simulated IC spread over public online graphs with random or uniform 0.5 weights. The built routes are greedy heuristics, so no RELINK result transfers to them. Any citation of 15% or 456/480 for Melange routes would be a misattribution.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper counts and code lines verified. Softened because the 15% claim is stated two ways in the paper ('up to' in the abstract, 'frequently exceeding' in Sec 6.3) and must be quoted as both. mc_spread uses Python random seeds, not the splitmix CRN, and only runs under MCMODE=1.

bearings.paper_claim: The IM-CSN objective is non-submodular (Introduction, citing Huang et al. 2022). The paper gives no optimality guarantee for its own policy and lists optimality under submodular objectives as future work (Sec 7). In Fig 4 (k=20, uniform weights) Random and PSNA generally perform best among baselines, followed by FoF and Degree. On dense graphs (email-Eu-core, wiki-Vote, sx-mathoverflow) PSNA beats RELINK at smaller seed sets (Sec 6.3, Fig 6).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 1 Introduction (non-submodularity, citing Huang et al.); Sec 6.2 Q1 and Fig 4 text; Sec 6.3 and Fig 6; Sec 7 future work
bearings.system_side: closedCascadeRoute grows a tree from the selected member with 6 edges and fanout 2 per recruiter (tpl line 947). Edge score is arrival x marginal x (0.75 + 0.25 PR/PRMAX) (line 842). Code comment at line 831 says IM-CSN is non-submodular, so no (1-1/e) claim. budgetRecruit is a node-coverage greedy that claims (1-1/e) on its coverage proxy (lines 773-777). The hub-convergence disclosure test is at line 525 of the test file.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The non-submodularity point and the warning that degree- or hub-favouring heuristics are weak under edge budgets carry over only as structural context. The paper's comparisons use public networks, mostly under IC with random weights, and its dense-graph losses to PSNA say nothing about the 533-member House graph. Hub convergence cannot be judged from the paper.
bearings.verifier_note: Ordering and win counts checked. Softened because the rel cites Sec 5.1 for non-submodularity, but that statement is in the Introduction. The test range 511-523 misses the hub-convergence test at line 525.

bearings.paper_claim: RELINK's learned edge policy is slower than PSNA on small and medium graphs and becomes competitive or often faster on large graphs, which the paper attributes to GPU inference and PSNA's complexity (Sec 6.2 Q3, Fig 5). Training took 6,257.329 s for 2,000 epochs because exact marginal gains are computed (Sec 6.4). The objective is non-submodular (Introduction).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 6.2 Q3 and Fig 5; Sec 6.4; Sec 1 Introduction
bearings.system_side: optimize.py is a lazy greedy over per-member chunks. Its docstring says that in a fixed stance state the objective is separable by member with diminishing returns, so greedy is the exact discrete allocation optimum. A Golovin-Krause bound is kept as a diagnostic. The dashboard budgetRecruit comment says no ML needed at our scale (tpl line 776).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper gives no graph-size threshold, so the tens-of-thousands figure in the rel is not from the paper. RELINK's case for a learned policy rests on scale and on non-submodular edge choice. The separable allocation in optimize.py is neither, so this paper neither supports nor refutes replacing greedy there. All benchmarks are synthetic-trained IC simulations.
bearings.verifier_note: Runtime and training-cost figures verified. Softened because 'tens of thousands of nodes' is not in the paper, 'CELF' does not appear in optimize.py (it says lazy greedy), and the non-submodular statement is in the Introduction rather than Sec 5.1.

bearings.paper_claim: Spread is estimated with 100,000 Monte Carlo IC simulations per selected subgraph, each experiment repeated 10 times, with averages reported (Sec 6.1). The paper gives no rationale for the number of draws. The 0.85 to 1.15 range is only the colour scale of the Fig 6 heatmap, not a claim about resolving method differences.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 6.1 Evaluation Criteria; Fig 6 colour scale (Sec 6.3)
bearings.system_side: Competitive IC uses keyed splitmix64 common random numbers (sm64 in moneyball_core.py around lines 549-553; build_P lines 555-562). MC default is 20 in budget_frontier.py line 7 and 40 in cosponsor_route.py line 25. The scenario MC setting was not checked.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's 100,000 draws are its own protocol and say nothing on whether 20 to 40 draws are adequate for Melange rank decisions. Adequacy remains the system's own claim (mc_stability_check), which this paper does not test. Any variance-reduction benefit of CRN is not supported by this paper.
bearings.verifier_note: Protocol numbers verified (100,000 draws, 10 repeats). The purpose clause in the rel bearing is not in the paper and is removed. Scenario MC not checked.

related.why: cosponsor_route.py cites RELINK together with MOPBD*. The linked item is titled Multi-Objective Path-Based D* Lite, so the link is via the code docstring, not via RELINK's own text.
Both are reinforcement-learning approaches to influence maximization. The link is topical; RELINK's text does not cite this item.
Reinforcement-learning influence maximization under complex contagion, a contrast with RELINK's IC-only setting. The link is topical, not a citation.
Learned policies for influence maximization when only sampled parts of the network are visible, a topical analogue of propagation restricted to chosen edges.
Graph embedding and graph neural networks for influence maximization, a topical link to RELINK's embedding pipeline.

Golovin-Krause style bounds rely on (adaptive) submodularity. RELINK says its IM-CSN objective is non-submodular, so those bounds do not carry over to edge-activation routes. Relation changed from contradicts, since RELINK does not dispute the theory.

Title concerns heuristic centrality methods challenging greedy optimization in influence maximization, a topical complement to RELINK's heuristic-versus-learned comparison. Whether it is the benchmark the dashboard cites was not verified.
Both use the Independent Cascade model with Monte Carlo spread estimation. Relation changed from same-data, since no data is shared. RELINK does not cite this item.

summary_issues: The claim that Melange kernel probabilities are mostly lower than the paper's regime was not checked against any kernel distribution.

The claim that the 533-member House cosponsor graph sits where RELINK's edge is smallest is unsupported. Its density was not computed, and the paper's dense-graph exceptions name only public networks.
The claim that both builds are close relatives of the baselines RELINK beats is a judgement, not a verified mapping.
Gap 1 says neither build was compared against a Random edge baseline. That is an absence claim checked only in the code, not in the wider repo or brain.
Gap 2 says mc_spread runs over every edge among selected nodes. That holds only when MCMODE=1, which is off by default, and the default route uses tree-reach.
The summary and flags say gains reach about 15%. The paper says up to 15% in the abstract and frequently exceeding 15% in Sec 6.3; both should be quoted.

paul_alignment and flags cite Paul's expectations (GCOMB for the optimizer, D* Lite and LPA* for replanning) and a brain entry (2026-06-feature-melange-scenario-model-build). No Paul markup or brain text was supplied or checked, so these are unverified.
